materials: one soft object {cat_name} already sleeps on or near
a small shallow dish
steps_template: Each evening at roughly the same hour, place the object in the spot near the front entry where {cat_name} tends to linger.
Sit nearby for two or three minutes without inviting {cat_name} over — let any approach happen on their own terms.
Leave the object in place overnight, undisturbed, for five consecutive nights.
On the sixth night, move the object two feet further from the door and repeat, gradually widening the claimed ground.
aftercare_note: A single missed night won't undo the pattern — consistency across most nights matters more than perfection on all of them.

materials: one small object {cat_name} already sleeps near
a pinch of dried catnip or valerian
a saucer or shallow dish
steps_template: At the same hour each evening, ideally as the light starts to change, bring the object and saucer to the entryway {cat_name} has been guarding or watching.
Set the object in the saucer just inside the boundary line.
Sit for the length of one song, roughly three minutes, without calling {cat_name} over.
Once {cat_name} approaches or settles nearby, say quietly: 'This edge is yours to keep, not yours to defend' — the words matter less than saying the same ones every night.
Leave the object in place overnight. Repeat for 7 nights running.
incantation_template: This edge is yours to keep, not yours to defend.
aftercare_note: If the guarding or watching fully stops before night 7, keep going anyway — the ritual is what makes the boundary feel earned, not just observed.

materials: a small enclosed bed or covered space
a worn piece of your clothing
steps_template: Before guests arrive, set up the enclosed bed in a low-traffic room and place your worn clothing inside it so it carries your scent.
Let {cat_name} explore and settle into this space on an ordinary day first, with no guests present, so it's already familiar before it's needed.
On the day of a gathering, close {cat_name} into that room with food, water, and litter access at least 30 minutes before guests arrive.
Check in quietly once, partway through, without forcing interaction.
aftercare_note: Release {cat_name} back into the main space only after guests have left and the noise has settled, not the moment the door closes.

materials: a small enclosed bed or covered space
a worn piece of your clothing
a white-noise source or fan
steps_template: Set up the enclosed safe space in the quietest room of the house, with your scent already on the bedding, at least three days before any planned gathering.
Run a white-noise source or fan in that room during ordinary days so the sound itself stops being novel.
On gathering days, move {cat_name} to the safe space a full hour before guests arrive, with food, water, and litter already inside.
For the first two gatherings, don't attempt any reintroduction at all — let the room be fully off-limits to guests.
From the third gathering onward, allow {cat_name} to choose to come out once things have quieted, never carried or coaxed out.
aftercare_note: Progress here is measured in weeks, not one event — a single calm gathering doesn't mean the pattern is resolved yet.

materials: your keys or coat, used as a neutral prop
one item of recently worn clothing
steps_template: Pick up your keys or coat, walk to the door, and then simply sit back down, two or three times a day, on days you aren't actually leaving.
Leave the worn clothing item in {cat_name}'s usual resting spot before any real departure.
When you do leave for real, keep the goodbye under five seconds — no prolonged reassurance, which reads as confirmation something's wrong.
On return, wait until {cat_name} is calm before greeting warmly — an excited reunion teaches the departure was worth being anxious about.
aftercare_note: Expect the practice departures to feel silly — that's fine, the repetition itself is the mechanism.

materials: your keys or coat, used as a neutral prop
one item of recently worn clothing
a food puzzle or slow-feeder
steps_template: Practice the full pre-departure routine — keys, coat, shoes — four or five times a day without actually leaving, at random times so it stops predicting anything.
Introduce a food puzzle only at real departure times, so {cat_name} associates the door closing with something engaging rather than only your absence.
Leave the worn clothing item in {cat_name}'s resting spot every time you leave, without exception, for the full two weeks.
Keep every goodbye and every greeting brief and low-key, even after a long day away.
Once panic at the door visibly eases, begin lengthening real absences gradually rather than jumping back to a full day away.
incantation_template: You are held, even in the quiet.
aftercare_note: A relapse after a disruption (travel, a schedule change) isn't a failure of the ritual — restart from day one of the practice-departure step.

materials: a fixed evening feeding time
a wind-down toy used only at that hour
steps_template: Pick one meal — ideally the last of the day — and serve it within the same 15-minute window every night, including weekends.
Immediately before that meal, run a five-minute play session with the wind-down toy, used at no other time of day.
After the meal, dim the lights in {cat_name}'s main resting area rather than leaving them at daytime brightness.
aftercare_note: Give this at least ten consecutive nights before judging whether it's working — a new rhythm doesn't register as reliable to a cat until it's been repeated many times.

materials: a fixed morning and evening feeding time
a wind-down toy used only at the evening hour
a food puzzle for overnight
steps_template: Fix two feeding times — morning and last-of-day — to the same 15-minute windows every day, weekends included, for the full three weeks.
Run a ten-minute active play session right before the evening meal, using a toy reserved only for that slot.
After the evening meal, set out a food puzzle that takes {cat_name} time and effort to empty, timed to land in the hour before your own bedtime.
Dim lights and reduce household activity in {cat_name}'s resting area at the same time each night.
Do not respond to nighttime vocalizing or activity by getting up to feed, play, or comfort — any response, even negative attention, reinforces the disruption.
aftercare_note: The overnight behavior is often the last thing to settle — expect the daytime rhythm to stabilize a week or more before nights fully calm.

materials: the existing anchor object
one consistent resting spot for it
steps_template: Choose one consistent spot for the object — not moved between locations — so {cat_name} can always find it in the same place.
Never wash, remove, or replace the object without first introducing a duplicate alongside it for at least a week.
When {cat_name} carries or settles with the object, let it happen without interference — this isn't a behavior to redirect.
aftercare_note: A strong attachment to one safe object is not, on its own, something to worry about — this ritual is about protecting the coping mechanism, not curing it.

title_template: The Investiture of the Anchor Object
materials: the existing anchor object
one consistent resting spot for it
a scent-matched duplicate
steps_template: Introduce a duplicate object early, worn in alongside the original by keeping both in {cat_name}'s bed for two weeks, so a loss of one isn't a loss of the coping mechanism itself.
Fix one consistent resting spot for whichever object is currently in use and never relocate it without cause.
If travel or washing requires the object's temporary absence, substitute the duplicate at least 48 hours beforehand rather than swapping it in cold.
Track whether the fixation is broadening (multiple objects) or narrowing (only ever this one) over several weeks — a broadening pattern is a good sign, a narrowing one is worth mentioning to a vet.
aftercare_note: This ritual doesn't aim to reduce the attachment — it aims to make sure the attachment never becomes a single point of failure.

materials: one additional food and water station
one additional litter box
steps_template: Add one more feeding station in a different room from the current one, out of direct line of sight of it.
Add one more litter box in a separate location, following the general rule of one box per cat plus one extra.
Feed {cat_name} at the added station for at least a week before judging whether the guarding behavior has eased.
aftercare_note: More stations only help if they're genuinely separated — two bowls three feet apart in the same room don't count as two options to a cat.

materials: multiple feeding stations in separate rooms
one litter box per cat plus one extra, in separate locations
vertical resting spaces near each station
steps_template: Map every current food, water, and litter location in the home, and identify which ones sit in shared or contested pathways.
Relocate or add stations so that no two are visible from one another, following the one-per-cat-plus-one rule for both food and litter.
Add at least one elevated resting spot near {cat_name}'s preferred station, giving a retreat option that doesn't require leaving the resource area.
For the first two weeks, feed {cat_name} at the same time as any other cats but at fully separated stations, rather than staggering times, so competition has no opportunity to form.
Once tension visibly eases, reintroduce more casual scheduling — but keep the physical separation permanently.
aftercare_note: This is a spatial fix more than a behavioral one — most of the work is in where things are, not what anyone does.

materials: a small mat or designated spot near where requests usually happen
steps_template: Place a small mat near the spot where {cat_name} usually vocalizes for attention (a doorway, the kitchen, a bedside).
Reward calm presence on the mat — quiet attention, a treat, a scratch — whenever {cat_name} chooses it over vocalizing.
When {cat_name} vocalizes for something you were about to give anyway (food, play), wait for a pause in the sound before responding, so silence — not noise — is what triggers the response.
aftercare_note: Expect vocalizing to briefly increase before it decreases — this is a normal 'extinction burst' as the old strategy is tested harder before it fades.

materials: a small mat or designated spot
two or three short scheduled play sessions
a treat reserved only for quiet-request rewards
steps_template: Establish three short, fixed-time play or attention sessions across the day, so {cat_name} has predictable engagement to rely on instead of vocalizing to request it.
Introduce a mat as the 'quiet request' spot and reward any calm presence there, using a treat reserved only for this purpose.
For demand-vocalizing outside the scheduled sessions, wait out a full pause in the sound — even a few seconds — before responding to anything, every time, without exception.
Never respond to vocalizing with the exact thing being demanded in the moment it's loudest — bridge every response through the pause-then-mat sequence.
Track which times of day the vocalizing clusters around, and make sure a scheduled session lands shortly before each one.
aftercare_note: Consistency matters more than any single step — one household member responding to loud demands undoes the pattern for everyone else.

materials: a soft brush
a quiet, low-traffic resting spot
steps_template: Once a day, at a consistent time, offer a short, gentle brushing session in {cat_name}'s quiet resting spot, stopping the moment {cat_name} shows any sign of wanting to stop.
Keep this resting spot free of loud activity, sudden guests, or other pets during the hour around the check-in.
Note, without intervening, whether self-grooming eases on days this check-in happens versus days it's skipped.
aftercare_note: The goal isn't to replace all self-grooming — it's to offer a lower-intensity outlet so grooming stops being the only available release.

title_template: The Release of the Held Voice
materials: a soft brush
a quiet, low-traffic decompression space
a food puzzle or slow-feeder
steps_template: Set up a dedicated low-stimulation space {cat_name} can retreat to at any time, kept free of loud noise, other pets, and sudden foot traffic.
Offer a gentle brushing session twice a day at consistent times, always stopping at the first sign {cat_name} wants to stop rather than pushing for a fixed duration.
Introduce a food puzzle during the hours grooming tends to spike, giving the same nervous energy a different outlet.
Reduce overall household noise and activity level during the two weeks of this ritual as much as is realistically possible.
If grooming intensity hasn't measurably eased after three weeks of consistent practice, treat that as a signal to involve a veterinarian rather than extending the ritual indefinitely.
incantation_template: What you cannot say, you do not have to carry alone.
aftercare_note: Progress here is usually gradual and uneven — judge it over weeks, not days, and don't be discouraged by an occasional bad night.

materials: three or four small toys
a storage box out of sight
steps_template: Keep only two or three toys out at any time, storing the rest out of sight.
Once a week, swap the available toys for a different set from storage, so nothing stays 'boring' from overexposure.
Run one five-to-ten-minute active play session daily, ending on a 'catch' so {cat_name} experiences a full hunt-catch cycle rather than stopping mid-chase.
aftercare_note: The rotation matters more than the toy count — a cat with twenty toys always out gets less novelty than one with three that change weekly.

materials: five or six toys of varying texture
a storage box out of sight
a foraging or puzzle feeder
steps_template: Divide toys into two or three rotating sets and swap the available set every four to five days.
Run two active play sessions daily, morning and evening, each ending on a real 'catch' so the hunt cycle completes rather than being cut short.
Introduce a foraging or puzzle feeder for at least one meal a day, so mealtime itself becomes a source of engagement for {cat_name} rather than a passive event.
Add one new, never-before-seen object (box, paper bag, textured mat) to the environment each week, removed after a few days before it becomes routine.
Track whether destructive or nighttime activity clusters around specific times of day, and place the active play session shortly before that window.
aftercare_note: If destructive behavior doesn't ease within two to three weeks of consistent enrichment, it's worth ruling out that the understimulation reading was actually the closest match.

materials: an existing favorite toy
five uninterrupted minutes
steps_template: Once a day, spend five minutes of fully undistracted attention with {cat_name} — no phone, no chores, just the toy or your hand and their choice of engagement.

Notice, once a week, whether anything from the quiz's themes (territory, sleep, social contact, objects, voice) has started to shift, since a steady reading today doesn't mean it stays steady forever.
Keep feeding, litter, and rest routines exactly as they currently are — the instruction here is to preserve the pattern, not to change it.
aftercare_note: A steady reading is a good result, not a null one — treat it as confirmation the current routine is working, worth protecting rather than second-guessing.
